grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: yo leo; tú lees; Luis lee. Yo escribo; tú escribes; Ana escribe. Yo quito; tú quitas; Ana quita.

tables.caption: la mesa · el suelo · el papel

grammar.note_en:
The present tense gives actions and states in the current scene. Last chapter’s regular -ar verbs had yo -o, tú -as and a named subject or usted -a. Regular verbs ending in -er or -ir have a different pattern in the singular: remove the infinitive ending and add -o for yo, -es for tú, and -e for a name or usted. Leer means “read”: its stem is le-, so le- + -o gives leo, le- + -es gives lees, and le- + -e gives lee. The two adjacent vowels are real: do not drop one. Escribir means “write”: escribo, escribes and escribe use the stem escrib-.

Escribo «mesa grande» means “I write ‘large table’”; ¿Qué escribes, Ana? means “What are you writing, Ana?”; Luis recibe el papel y lee means “Luis receives the paper and reads”. ¿Qué lees tú? is “What do you read?” or “What are you reading?” Leo «mesa grande» means “I read ‘large table’”. These forms differ from the -ar pattern even when both forms end in a similar sound: tú escribes has -es, whereas tú llevas has -as. The spelling tells you which verb family is involved. An infinitive is the dictionary form naming a verb; the infinitives here are cues, not commands.

Vivir, “live”, has vivo, vives and vive. Yo vivo aquí means “I live here”; ¿Vives en la casa roja? means “Do you live in the red house?” The home is Elena’s residence; the shared reading room is not thereby her property. Comer, “eat”, gives como, comes and come. ¿Tú comes aquí, Elena? means “Do you eat here, Elena?” Yo como aquí means “I eat here”. Beber, “drink”, gives bebo, bebes and bebe. ¿Bebes agua, Luis? means “Are you drinking water, Luis?” Yo bebo agua means “I drink water”. A Spanish present form can cover English simple and progressive descriptions; no extra helper is needed for “is drinking”.

Recibir means “receive”. Luis recibe la pata means “Luis receives the leg”: the object changes hands. Subir here means moving something upwards. Yo subo la caja means “I raise the box”; ¿Tú subes el libro, Ana? means “Are you lifting the book, Ana?” Subo el libro means “I lift the book”. The context contrasts the floor with a chair or the characters’ hands. Subir can have other uses, but this chapter’s cards teach this demonstrated sense. Quitar is a regular -ar verb, “remove”: Yo quito una pata means “I remove a leg”; ¿Tú quitas otra? means “Are you removing another?” Do not give quitar an -er ending merely because the other new action verbs use -er or -ir.

Cabe is the only form of caber, “fit”, introduced here. La mesa no cabe en la puerta means “The table does not fit through the doorway”. La pata cabe en la puerta means “The leg fits through the doorway”. Fitting concerns available space; pasar describes actually passing through. A detached leg can pass where the whole table cannot; removing all four legs changes the table’s shape and makes transport possible. The rest of caber is not regular in all persons, so do not generate its other forms from this chapter’s regular pattern.

Pata is a furniture leg; four patas support this table. Alto/alta and bajo/baja describe height: La mesa es alta means “The table is high”; es baja means “it is low”. Agreement still follows the noun: mesa is feminine, so alta and baja end in -a; suelo, “floor”, is masculine, so El suelo está seco means “The floor is dry” and El suelo está mojado means “The floor is wet”. El papel está seco means “The paper is dry”; el papel está mojado means “The paper is wet”. Las manos mojadas means “the wet hands”. These states do not follow automatically from an object’s colour or age.

Agua, “water”, is a feminine noun, although its singular article here is el: el agua. This special article occurs before the stressed initial a sound. The article does not make the noun masculine. This chapter does not ask for an adjective form with agua; learn its gender and its actual article together. Without an article, Ana bebe agua means “Ana drinks water”, referring to water as a substance. The water given during the break and the later wet patch are observations; the chapter has not yet established the source of the water on the floor.

The table’s remaining cells mean “I write / you write / Ana writes”, “I live / you live / Elena lives”, “I drink / you drink / Ana drinks”, and “I raise / you raise / Luis raises”. La mesa es baja means “The table is low”. El papel está seco and El papel está mojado mean “The paper is dry” and “The paper is wet”.
